analysis.one_liner: Expands health coverage for low-income pregnant women, adds patient protections for children, and funds pediatric research and poison control centers.
analysis.headline: This bipartisan children's health bill, backed by the sponsor and 23 cosponsors from both parties, never received a House vote; it sat in three committees and their subcommittees until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let states cover low-income, uninsured pregnant women through the Children's Health Insurance Program, with automatic coverage for their newborns for the first year of life. It would add patient rights to employer-based health plans — including direct access to obstetricians and pediatric specialists without gatekeeper referrals, and an independent appeal process for denied care for children. It also funds children's hospitals that train doctors, a CDC center for birth defects research, safe-motherhood monitoring, a national poison control hotline, and pediatric research at the National Institutes of Health.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income pregnant women who would gain insurance coverage for prenatal, delivery, and postpartum care, and their babies, who would be automatically enrolled in children's health coverage for their first year. Children in employer health plans would gain faster access to OB/GYN and pediatric specialist care and an outside appeal when a plan denies treatment. Children's hospitals, poison control centers, and pediatric researchers would gain new federal funding.

how_it_helps.text: States could optionally cover pregnancy-related care for targeted low-income uninsured pregnant women under their Children's Health Insurance Program plans, with no pre-existing condition exclusions or waiting periods.
A child born to a woman receiving that pregnancy coverage would be deemed automatically enrolled in child health assistance until age one, removing a paperwork gap at the most vulnerable moment.

Employer-based group health plans would have to let patients see an obstetrician or gynecologist without a primary-care referral, let parents designate a pediatrician as their child's primary provider, send children needing specialty care to qualified specialists — covering out-of-network specialists at in-network cost when the plan lacks one — and provide an independent external review of denied claims for children's care.
Children's hospitals would receive direct and indirect medical education payments, set at $95 million plus $190 million per year for fiscal years 2001 through 2003, to train pediatricians.

The bill funds a CDC National Center for Birth Defects Research and Prevention, programs on prenatal smoking, alcohol, and drug use, safe-motherhood monitoring in all 50 states, a nationwide poison control hotline with a $25 million annual grant program, and a $100 million-per-year pediatric research initiative at NIH with loan repayment for pediatric researchers.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers would fund the new grants, hospital payments, and research authorizations, which total several hundred million dollars a year. Self-insured employers and their health plans would bear the cost of the new patient-access rules and external appeals in their coverage of children. The CHIP pregnancy coverage would come out of states' existing federal allotments, potentially competing with coverage for children.

drawbacks.text: The pregnancy coverage is optional for states and expressly does not increase the federal allotments states receive, so states would have to fund it by redirecting money within existing CHIP budgets, potentially at the expense of children's coverage.

The patient-rights requirements apply only to self-insured group plans and expressly not to fully insured plans, which are regulated by states instead — so many families with insured coverage would not get the same protections.
New benefit and access mandates on employer health plans add to plan administrative and coverage costs, a cost that ultimately shows up in premiums and wages.

The bill authorizes substantial new federal spending — roughly $300 million a year for children's hospital training alone, plus grants for CDC programs, poison centers, and NIH research — adding to the federal budget.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are concrete: prenatal coverage, automatic newborn enrollment, and faster access to specialists for sick children. The costs are real but modest relative to the scale — the CHIP expansion is optional and capped by existing allotments, and the mandate costs fall on a subset of employer plans. The bill's main design weakness is its state-by-state optionality and the exemption of fully insured plans from the new rights, which limits how many families actually benefit.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to three House committees and then to three subcommittees in the spring of 1999, and none of them ever acted on it, so it never reached a vote before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Jo Ann Emerson (R-MO) introduced the Healthy Kids 2000 Act on March 11, 1999.

The Speaker referred it to three committees — Commerce, Ways and Means, and Education and the Workforce — splitting it among panels with jurisdiction over health programs, employer health plans, and entitlements.

Within a month it was sent down to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health, the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and the Education and Workforce Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations.
Twenty-three representatives signed on as cosponsors, 16 Democrats and 7 Republicans, but no committee held a markup and the House never voted on the bill.
No further action appears in the record after the April 1999 subcommittee referrals, and the 106th Congress ended without the bill advancing.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employer health plans and the businesses that fund them avoided new patient-access rules and external appeals for children's coverage, and federal spending on children's hospitals, poison control centers, and pediatric research never materialized. Low-income pregnant women and sick children — the bill's intended beneficiaries — received nothing from it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employer health plans; intended beneficiaries got nothing

sides.party_line_note: The sponsorship was bipartisan: of the 23 cosponsors, 16 were Democrats and 7 were Republicans, and the sponsor was a Republican — there is no sign the bill died along party lines, only that committees declined to act on it.

industries.note: The bill would have created a dedicated federal payment stream — $95 million for direct and $190 million for indirect training costs per year in fiscal years 2001-2003 — for children's hospitals that train pediatric residents. Because it died, these hospitals kept training future pediatricians without this dedicated support, and the pipeline of children's doctors it was meant to expand never got the funding.

industries.industry: Employer health plans and self-insured employers
industries.note: The bill would have required self-insured employer plans to grant direct OB/GYN and pediatric specialist access, cover out-of-network specialists at in-network cost when the plan lacks one, and submit to independent external review of denied children's claims. Because the bill died, these plans continued to operate without those obligations.

The bill would have stabilized their funding with $25 million a year in grants, a national toll-free number, and a public awareness campaign, citing their cost-effectiveness — $7 in saved medical costs per dollar spent. The centers continued to consolidate and close for lack of stable funding.
